title: Before the cock crows twice (Mark 14:53–72)
hookLine: Jesus is silent before the council; Peter weeps

cards: Three denials, spoken by a fire in the dark. Each one is said to protect himself, by the man who swore, only hours before, that he would never fall away.
In the middle of the night they take Jesus to the high priest's house, where the chief priests and elders gather. And Peter, who ran away with the others, comes back.
He follows at a distance, right into the courtyard, and sits with the servants, warming himself by the fire. Upstairs, a trial. Downstairs, by the fire, another one.

teach.b: First, the silence. Inside, witnesses accuse Jesus, but their stories don't agree. The high priest stands up and demands an answer.
In the Douay-Rheims: "But he held his peace, and answered nothing." Jesus, who's been talking all through Mark, says nothing to the accusations. Second, the answer.

teach.h: ARE YOU THE CHRIST? I AM.
teach.b: The high priest asks him straight: are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus, with no hedging at all: "I am." You shall see the Son of man at the right hand of power.
It's called blasphemy, and some begin to spit on him and strike him. Third, the fire. Downstairs, a servant girl looks at Peter in the firelight: you were with the Nazarene.
He says he doesn't know what she means. She tells the others; he denies it again. Then the bystanders: surely you're one of them.

teach.h: BY THE FIRE: I KNOW NOT THIS MAN.
teach.b: And Peter begins to curse and swear: "I know not this man of whom you speak." Upstairs, Jesus says I am. Downstairs, Peter says I'm not.
Fourth, the tears. "And immediately the cock crew again."

teach.h: THE COCK CROWS, AND PETER WEEPS.
teach.b: Peter remembers the word, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt thrice deny me.
"And he began to weep." An early tradition, from a bishop named Papias, says Mark wrote down what Peter preached. If that's right, this story most likely came from Peter's own mouth.
The man Catholics call the first pope told it on himself, and the Gospel kept it.

how: Catholics bring their sins to the sacrament of confession, and Peter's denial and tears are often held up in Catholic preaching as a picture of sorrow that leads back to mercy rather than despair.

o: breaking the rules of the Sabbath day
lying under oath in front of a judge
speech that insults or dishonors God

games.q: two trials at once — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus argues back against every accusation
"he held his peace, and answered nothing."
the bystanders say Peter must be one of them because he is a Galilean
the third time, they tell him he must be one of them, since he is also a Galilean.
an early tradition says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching
Papias, an early bishop, says so, which would mean Peter told this story on himself.

games.q: you're Peter by the fire. a servant girl says, you were with the Nazarene. what do you say?
o: yes, I was. arrest me too.
I don't know what you mean.
games.why: he denies it three times, the last with curses: "I know not this man of whom you speak." then the cock crows, and he weeps.

practice: Bring back one moment you've regretted, when you protected yourself and someone else paid for it, and just remember it, the way Peter remembered the word: don't relive the details, don't defend yourself.
If tears come, let them; if not, let there be quiet, because being sorry is not the same as being finished, and Peter's story didn't end by the fire. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God.

wordCard.voice: Blasphemy. What the high priest calls it when Jesus answers the elders plainly, I am, just before Peter, downstairs, denies him three times. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he wept, in a tense that suggests he kept on weeping.

carryVoice: Your line: peter wept. The rooster crowed, and he remembered. Day two hundred twenty-eight, done.
